timecoded_text_to_speech.text: So we're out here in San Francisco in the Bay Area at SOCAP, one of the world's largest
convenings at the intersection of money and meaning, and today it's a real privilege.
Because we're here with Van Jones, who is globally recognized, catalyst, best-selling author,
both in the clean jobs arena as well as human rights.
He's served in the White House with the Obama Administration.
He's also a serial entrepreneur himself having launched three successful nonprofit organizations.
But to put it under a broad umbrella, I'd say catalyst, movement maker, iconoclastic,
you know, incredible, incredible man and entrepreneur.
So with that said, Van, I'm just curious, what are you doing here at SOCAP?
What drives you to this community?
So I wanted to come here and be around folks who really understand that we can build
the future that we want.
I think the two big crises right now are spiritual and economic.
And this is a place that's trying to deal with both at the same time.
How do you use a power-wrenching for Northship to identify and solve problems?
But how do you make sure some of the problems that you're solving are problems for humanity
and for the planet?
And not just problems of your own pocketbook, not being full enough.
And so it's a great place for me to be.
What's got you on fire right now?
What's the thing that you're thinking about in the show and that's keeping you up at night?
My love for democracy and wanting to see a counterbalance in our society to what the
Tea Party has been able to achieve.
And so we're creating this thing called the American Dream Movement.
And so we progress at Page Freed to stick up for the American Dream.
And we're building a platform called RebuildTheDream.com to support the American Dream Movement.
The same way that Freedom Works and America's For Prosperity and Liberty Labs support the
Tea Party Movement.
And so entrepreneurship isn't just in the marketplace for consumers.
Entrepreneurship is also in the civic space for citizens.
And that's really what I've loved to be a part of.
How is technology playing into this?
How are you leveraging the new explosions in the ability to bring together crowds and
so on with technology?
Well it is just a great time to be an entrepreneur.
The low cost high leverage tools that are available to you are just unbelievable.
I think people need context and community for information.
And technology I think we should see it more as a digital campfire that we're trying
to build community around.
And the most important thing is what are the stories we're telling on that campfire?
And in terms of seems that everything you're talking about is values driven.
Very much so.
How do you stumble upon that value that drives you beyond just productivity and innovation?
See the thing is, whatever you're doing, whatever you're selling, half the time there's 12
other people doing the same thing.
And so a differentiator can come if you can add some more meaning to it.
And I think you're going to see more and more people, especially some of the top end consumers.
They're going to be purchasing meaning.
They want to badge themselves.
As long as your customer is just looking for value, somebody can out compete.
They're looking for value plus values.
You can always have that relationship.
And that's I think how you got to look at this entrepreneur.
I'm just curious, what is the most difficult part about what you're working on right now,
what you're working towards?
Well, I mean, I pretty much live in airports now.
You know, it's metaphor my life now is just sort of being in airplane.
And I'm not where I want to be and I'm not where I was.
This past month I've been home a lot more, which feels good.
But I'm also working on a book so then that cuts into the time.
I mean, part of the thing and I think the challenge is you better make sure what you're working on.
You're working on for more than money.
What's going to happen to you if you're just doing it for money is when you're runs over
and you're in the deathbed or whatever the thing is, you're going to have a lot of regret.
Because the money's just not worth it.
I mean, I've had money, I've not had money.
But what makes life worth it is a community that you build, it's relationships that you have,
it's a contribution that you make.
And very few people at the end of their life say I wish I worked harder to make money.
They're very few people at the end of their lives.
Yeah, very few people in the life say I wish I worked harder to make more money to leave
to my family, to leave to a charity or to leave my bank account or to leave for them
to fight over in the wills and that, no.
Most people say I wish I spent more time with people I cared about.
My challenge at the social entrepreneurs is I love my family and I also see a big extended
family called humanity that I'm always trying to balance my responsibilities too.
Yeah.
Well, man, thank you so much.
You had a real privilege.
Yeah, appreciate you.
I look forward to the next conversation.
Thank you.
Looking forward to it as well.

youtube_description:
Van Jones discusses the following points with Daniel Epstein of the Unreasonable Institute:
- Spiritual and economic crisis
- Solving problems with entrepreneurship for humanity, not just -pocketbook
- Rebuildthedream.com as counter movement to Tea Party
- Entrepreneurship not just as capital gain, but as social gain for human rights
- Low cost, high leverage tools 
- Technology as digital camp fire - what are the stories we're telling?
- Value-driven choices
- Stand out by giving deeper meaning
- Working for more than money
- Humanity as our extended family
youtube_title: Interview: Van Jones, Rebuild the Dream
